summary:
Moonbase Command is a free browser game in which kids aged 7 to 12 lead a Moon base or Mars outpost through a 10-day mission. Each day they share five energy blocks between life support, the radiation shield and the greenhouse lab. There is never enough for everything, so no choice is free: shielding the crew costs air or food, and a big research day leaves thinner air tomorrow.

It addresses the challenge by turning real mission constraints into play. Every solar storm is a real 2017 solar flare listed in NASA's DONKI database, shown with its date and class. Radiation adds up and never goes down, food takes three days to grow, and on Mars, answers from Earth arrive late. Poor decisions lead to a sick crew, damaged panels or an aborted mission, always with an explanation.

This matters because children usually see only the outcomes of space missions. Here they experience the reasoning behind them, and learn that exploration means weighing risks with limited resources.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Moonbase Command is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player commands a Moon base or a Mars outpost with three astronauts for a 10-day mission. Every day follows three steps: read the morning report, share out five energy blocks between life support, the radiation shield and the greenhouse lab, then see what happened. There is never enough energy for everything. Each mission also draws a task, such as earning research stars or leaving food for the next crew.

The solar storms are real. Each mission replays an actual 10-day period from 2017, and every storm is a solar flare listed in NASA's DONKI database, shown with its date and flare class. The flare class sets the storm strength in the game.

Decisions have consequences. Radiation adds up and never goes down. A storm that gets through the shield sends the crew to the shelter and can damage a solar panel. Thin air makes the crew tired, hunger and sickness raise the risk of accidents, and food planted today is only ready three days later. If the crew's health is at risk, mission control aborts the mission and explains exactly why. On Mars, the base cannot see how strong a storm is: asking Earth costs energy and the answer arrives a day late.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Children usually see the results of space missions, not the reasoning behind them. This game lets them make the trade-offs themselves and learn from the outcome. It explains the situation without giving the answer: a live forecast shows what a plan will do, a food plan makes delays visible, and optional hints point to what to look at. A mission report judges mission, task and crew safety separately from the research score. The game needs no download and no account, so it works at home and in classrooms.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

HTML, CSS and JavaScript without frameworks, built into a single self-contained file. Graphics are drawn in SVG, music and sound effects are generated in the browser with the Web Audio API. The game rules are pure functions covered by 35 automated tests run with Node.js, including a search over every possible plan to prove that each mission can be completed. The game is hosted on GitHub Pages. Some of the program code, the graphics, the music and sound effects, and the texts were generated with the AI assistant Claude (Anthropic). Our team chose the challenge, directed the design, playtested the game with children and decided what to change. No AI model runs inside the game.

CREATIVITY

The base is a living scene: astronauts walk around, answer when tapped and react to the state of the mission. Real space weather drives the story of each mission, and failure is treated as part of learning, with an explanation instead of a game over.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Readability for young children, honesty about what is real data and what is simplified, accessibility by touch, mouse and keyboard, and fairness: every mission is winnable without luck. We playtested with children and reworked the introduction, the meters and the event texts based on their feedback.
